title: ILJAZOVIC v. SWEDEN
summary: In the case of Iljazovic v. Sweden, the applicants—Aleksander, Stefan, Marija, and Filip Iljazovic—are Serbian nationals who identified themselves as Roma, a group encompassed by the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. Their case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma children facing the threat of deportation to Serbia, where they alleged a lack of family support and inadequate state protection due to their ethnicity. The Iljazovic children arrived in Sweden with their parents in December 2006 and sought asylum, citing years of ethnic persecution in Serbia and the authorities’ refusal to protect them. After their father was murdered in 2008 and their mother was imprisoned for complicity, the children were placed with relatives in Sweden. Despite these traumatic events and their claims of having no caregivers in Serbia, Swedish authorities repeatedly rejected their asylum requests, concluding that Serbian authorities could provide adequate protection. The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 8 (right to family life), fearing separation from their mother and lack of care if deported. However, after the Swedish Migration Board granted them permanent residence permits in October 2009, the Court struck the case out, as the applicants no longer faced deportation. This case underscores the precarious situation of Roma children in asylum proceedings and reflects ongoing challenges faced by Roma and Traveller families seeking protection in Europe.
